newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Uzbeks rally behind general's threat to Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Uzbeks rally behind general's threat to Taleban.

text.p: Pride and patriotism surged through the dusty bazaars of Mazar-i-Sharif on Monday after the region's Uzbek warlord vowed to fight to prevent further advances by Taleban forces into northern Afghanistan.
"Of course, all of us are happy that someone has stood up to the Taleban and especially those of us women who work," said Shema, a gynaecologist at the city's public hospital.

"I've spent six years traning to be a doctor, but if Taleban enter this city I will not be allowed to work. Afghanistan needs peace most of all, but not a Taleban peace made by the Pashtuns for the Pashtuns. We will support our general even if it means fighting."

Uzbek strongman General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who controls six of Afghanistan's northern provinces, warned on Sunday he would fight the Taleban, who captured Kabul on September 27, if they continued their attack against the Panjsher valley northeast of the capital.

Taleban's ultra-conservative interpretation of Islam and its Pashtun ethnic flavour have rung alarm bells throughout northern Afghanistan, especially among Uzbeks and Tajiks whose military leaders were at odds until recently.

Dostum and Ahmad Shah Masood -- the Tajik military chief of government forces recently routed from Kabul by Taleban, and the man now directing the defence of the Panjsher Valley -- seem ready to cooperate against what they see as a common threat.

Wily survivors of nearly two decades of conflict in Afghanistan, the two men working together would represent a potent military force. Dostum's men are well equipped and the closest thing Afghanistan has to a proper fighting force.
Masood managed to retreat to the Panjsher with most of his armour and artillery intact, and the two commanders would have the advantage of fighting defensively on their own rugged mountain terrain.
"Dostum and Masood are not friends, they are enemies, but now they will work together to stop the Taleban," explained Ali, a taxi driver sipping tea with friends at a roadside stand.
"We remember what happened with the Pashtuns before. Uzbeks and Tajiks will never let them into the north again. They cannot defeat us if we are together."

Pashtuns, viewed as a "southern" tribe by northerners, overthrew the Afghan king in the 1920s and established a reign of terror in the north that included massacres, rapes and the enforced study of Pashtun language in local schools.
Uzbeks and Tajiks later regained control of their areas, but speak of the time of the Pashtun as though it were yesterday.

Northerners also speak critically of Pakistani support for the Taleban and brand the movement that now controls about three-quarters of Afghanistan's 33 provinces as a mere stalking horse for Islamabad.

But nowhere is fear of the Taleban more concentrated than among educated urban women. They are horrified by the ban, in Kabul and elsewhere, on working or attending school and venturing outside the home unless traditionally dressed in veil or are escorted.

"The fear among women who work for us and with us is that if the Taleban reach Mazar-i-Sharif, it will be straight off with their heads," Samantha Reynolds, regional manager of the U.N. Habitat programme, told Reuters on Monday.
"It is very sobering for our staff to have to assess their participation in that light," she said.
